About this simulation

Physics: The Stern-Gerlach experiment measures spin along a chosen axis. Z-magnets split atoms into Z+ and Z−, while X-magnets split into X+ and X−. Switching measurement axis changes the state basis, so prior spin information along a different axis is no longer definite.

Visuals: The 3D view shows the atom source, magnet stages, optional blockers, beam branching, and detector hits. Beam direction and color encode the current spin channel, and the legend maps colors to unpolarized, Z, and X outcomes.

Controls: Build Stage 2/3 by dragging magnets or blockers, set Stage 1 orientation/blocker, tune emission rate and field strength, and use play/pause, reset, and stats controls. Turn on Explore to see hover explanations on apparatus parts.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Sequential stages

Here’s the twist on the classic experiment: instead of just a single stage, we’re going to line up several Stern–Gerlach stages in a row. A Z magnet measures the spin component along z and an X magnet measures it along x; each deflects a beam according to the value it measures. And a blocker placed after a magnet stops one of that magnet’s two output beams.

2 · A second magnet

Let’s add a second magnet. An X magnet now stands after the first Z magnet. What do you think — how many regions of the detector screen are lit up?

3 · One output blocked

Now let’s measure the same thing twice. The spin-down (↓) output of the first Z magnet is blocked, and a Z magnet occupies the second slot. What’s your guess — how many regions of the detector screen are lit up?

4 · A third stage

One last experiment, and it’s the big one. The ↓ output of the first Z magnet is still blocked. An X magnet follows, with its ← output blocked. A Z magnet fills the third slot. Think it through carefully — how many regions of the detector screen are lit up?

01

At a glance

A Stern–Gerlach magnet sorts silver atoms by one component of their spin. This sim sends atoms through up to three magnet stages, with optional blockers, onto a screen, so you can build a chain and see what each stage does. It is the standard first example of measurement in quantum mechanics.

What you'll learn

  • What a Stern–Gerlach magnet measures, and what the Z and X settings mean.
  • How a blocker, and a second or third magnet, change which atoms reach the screen.
  • How to work out the number of spots and the fraction of atoms detected for any chain.
  • What the field strength and the emission rate change.
Atoms travel left to right. Stages 2 and 3 are optional (dashed); a blocker removes atoms after a stage.

What's on screen

  • Unpolarized atoms (lime): atoms before the first magnet.
  • Atoms after a magnet, coloured by the last value measured: Z+ ↑ rose, Z− ↓ blue, X+ → violet, X− ← teal.
  • Blocker (red): stops the atoms with the value it names.
  • Screen: a spot marks each landing position. A spot's glow fades after about 10 s; the mark stays.
  • Statistics (side panel): counts of atoms emitted, detected and blocked, and the final + and − values.
See itRun one Z magnet at 0.40 T. Watch for: atoms changing colour as they pass the magnet, and spots building up on the screen.

03

What one magnet measures

A Stern–Gerlach magnet has a field that changes across its gap, so it pushes on an atom's magnetic moment. The push depends on the component of the moment along the magnet's axis, and on nothing else about the atom.

The force on the atom, and the values the silver atom's moment can take (electron g-factor taken as 2).
  • Silver's moment comes from one unpaired electron. Along any one axis it can only take the two values ∓μB, so each atom is pushed one of two ways.
  • In the sim, Z magnets deflect atoms up or down on the screen and X magnets left or right. ↑ lands on top because the field grows downward across the gap (∂Bz/∂z < 0). Flip the magnet and ↑ and ↓ swap sides.
  • Atoms leave the source unpolarized. At the first magnet each atom gets ↑ or ↓ with equal chance, drawn independently.
Key idea. After a magnet, each atom has the value that magnet measured, and where it lands on the screen tells you which value.
See itRun one Z magnet at 0.40 T and watch the two counters. Watch for: rose spots above blue spots, with Final + and Final − staying close to each other.
04

Repeating a measurement

Block the ↓ output of a Z magnet and every atom that gets past it has Sz = +ħ/2. Put a second Z magnet after it and the same question is asked again.

The same axis again: the same answer with probability 1, so nothing splits.
  • Every atom is found ↑ again. A measurement that is repeated straight away gives the same result; this is what lets us call it a measurement.
  • The sim applies this as a rule: when a stage measures the same axis as the stage before it, the atom keeps its value.
  • The beam is pushed again, so the spot lands farther from the centre than for one magnet: 5.21 units at 0.40 T, against 3.24.
  • Without the blocker, Z then Z still gives two spots, one for each value. Each atom keeps what it had.
See itRun Z with ↓ blocked, then a second Z magnet. Watch for: a single rose spot, and Final − staying at 0.
05

A different axis starts over

An atom with a definite Sz does not have a definite Sx. In the standard description its state is an equal mix of the two Sx states:

The X magnet gets probability ½ for each of its two results.
  • The sim follows this: a stage that measures a different axis from the one before it gives each atom a fresh 50/50 result.
  • So Z followed by X splits each Z beam again, and four spots appear in a 2 × 2 pattern: Z results move a spot vertically, X results horizontally.
  • Each stage acts on whatever reaches it. Counting spots means following every beam through every stage.
Key idea. The result of the Z magnet does not predict the result of the X magnet. Each new axis is a new 50/50 draw.
See itRun a Z magnet followed by an X magnet at 0.40 T. Watch for: four separate spots building up on the screen, in a 2 × 2 pattern.
06

How a blocked value comes back

Take Z with ↓ blocked, then X with ← blocked, then Z. Two blockers are in place, and still some atoms reach the screen with ↓: the value Stage 1 removed.

Each box is a stage; the red bars are the blockers.
  • Each atom passes Stage 1 with probability ½, passes Stage 2 with ½, and gets ↑ or ↓ at Stage 3 with ½ each. Each final spot gets ⅛ of the emitted atoms.
  • In the standard description, the X magnet leaves the atom with a definite Sx and no definite Sz. The last magnet's ↓ is a new result, not a label the atom kept.
  • The order matters because Sx and Sz do not commute: [Ŝx, Ŝz] = −iħŜy.
  • Take the X magnet out and the effect stops: Z with ↓ blocked, then Z, gives one spot (section 04).
See itRun Z (↓ blocked), X (← blocked), then Z. Watch for: Final − rising above 0 although Stage 1 blocked ↓, and a blue spot just below a rose one.
07

Counting atoms and spots

Build any chain in the sim and the panel follows it.

rate field

These sliders move the sim too. Moving the field clears the counters.

  • Walk down the chain. A magnet splits what reaches it into two branches of ½ each, unless the atoms already have a value along its axis. A blocker deletes one branch.
  • Multiply the ½s along a path to get the fraction of emitted atoms in that spot.
  • Spot positions are in direct proportion to the field. At 0.00 T every beam lands at the centre, so there is one spot.
  • The field changes where atoms land, not how many. The emission rate changes how fast the counters fill, not the fractions.
See itRun Z then X at 0.10 T, then at 0.50 T. Watch for: the same four-spot pattern in both runs, five times wider in the second.
08

Where it matters

  • Frankfurt, 1922. Stern and Gerlach sent a silver-atom beam through an inhomogeneous magnetic field onto a plate. A moment free to point any way would leave a continuous band. They found two separate lines.
  • Spin, identified afterwards. Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit proposed electron spin in 1925, and the two lines were then read as the two spin states of silver's single outer electron.
  • Atomic-beam methods. Rabi's and Ramsey's magnetic-resonance methods, and early caesium beam clocks, used inhomogeneous magnets to select and detect atoms by their spin or hyperfine state.
  • Teaching measurement. Chains of Stern–Gerlach stages are the standard way to introduce measurement and non-commuting observables.
Go deeper: how big is the real splitting
Illustrative round numbers, not the values of the 1922 apparatus. Δu is the shift of each beam; the two beams are 2Δu apart.
A classical moment would fill a band; the plate showed two lines.
  • The real splitting is tiny: with these inputs the beams end up about 0.14 mm apart. The sim's spots are much farther apart so they can be seen.
  • The sim itself does not compute this estimate. It draws a deflection in proportion to the field slider.
09

Summary

In one line. A Stern–Gerlach magnet sorts atoms by one spin component. The same axis again repeats the result; a different axis starts a new ½–½ split.

Key points

  • Where an atom lands tells you the value its last magnet measured.
  • A magnet on a different axis splits each beam ½ and ½, so a blocked value can come back (⅛ in the example).
  • Multiply the ½s along a path to count atoms; the field only sets how far apart the spots are.

Common mix-ups

  • "The X magnet only hides the atom's Z value." In the standard description there is no Z value left to hide.
  • "Blocking ↓ removes spin-down atoms for good." Only at that stage. After an X magnet, a later Z magnet gives ↓ to half the atoms again.
  • "A stronger field gives a cleaner result." It only moves the spots apart; every probability stays the same.

Things to try on your own

  • Build Z (↓ blocked) then Z, and Z (↓ blocked), X, then Z. Compare the spots and counters with the panel in section 07.
  • Set Field Strength to 0.00 T with a blocker in place, and note which counters still change.
  • Build X then Z, and compare its pattern with Z then X.
